questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: What a key signature holds
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a key signature records and how it is applied
questions.stem: The survey notes that the recordings carry one sharp on the F line. What does that key signature tell the reader?

options.text: That every F in the passage is raised a semitone unless marked otherwise.
That the passage is in F major and should always end on that note.
options.misconception: Believes the signature names the final note of the melody

options.text: That only the first F of each phrase is raised by a semitone.
options.misconception: Believes the accidental applies to a single note

options.text: That the F lines are inaudible and can be ignored when scoring calls.
options.misconception: Believes the signature removes notes from the score

questions.explanation: A key signature is a standing instruction to alter every occurrence of the listed letters, so a sharp on F raises each F unless cancelled. It neither names the final note nor limits itself to one pitch.
questions.hint: It applies to every matching letter name.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Why the circle of fifths is ordered as it is
questions.learningObjective: Explain the ordering principle behind the circle of fifths
questions.stem: The survey plots call pitch classes around a circle to compare neighbouring sites. Explain why the circle of fifths is drawn in that order.

answer.exemplar: The circle of fifths arranges keys so that each one is a perfect fifth from the next, which means each step around the circle adds one sharp or removes one flat from the signature. The order therefore makes the number of accidentals grow by one per step, lets any key be reached by moving clockwise for sharps or anticlockwise for flats, and keeps closely related keys close together on the diagram.

questions.explanation: Moving a perfect fifth at a time adds or removes exactly one accidental, so the circle makes the growing accidentals visible and keeps related keys adjacent. That is the whole point of its ordering.
questions.hint: Each step is a perfect fifth.

questions.stem: A transcription ends with a note that lies a semitone below the repeated tonic pitch. What is that note called?

options.text: The leading tone, because it sits a semitone below the tonic and pulls toward it.
The subtonic, because it lies a whole step below the tonic pitch.
options.misconception: Confuses a whole step below with a semitone below

options.text: The mediant, because it is the third degree of the scale.
options.misconception: Names the third degree instead of the seventh

options.text: The tonic itself, because the survey resolves the phrase on that note.
options.misconception: Treats the resolution note as the tonic

questions.explanation: The seventh degree raised to a semitone below the tonic is the leading tone, and its half step distance gives it its strong pull upward. A whole step below the tonic would instead be the subtonic.
questions.hint: A half step below the home note.

options.text: Dominant, because it is the chord that pushes toward the return to the tonic.
Subdominant, because it precedes the dominant in a typical phrase.
options.misconception: Names the chord that comes before the dominant

options.text: Tonic, because the phrase returns to that chord at the end.
options.misconception: Confuses the destination with the pushing chord

options.text: Mediant, because it sits between tonic and dominant by position.
options.misconception: Reads a chord's position as its function

questions.explanation: The dominant is the chord with the strongest pull toward the tonic, so a chord that pushes toward the return is dominant. The subdominant does the opposite job, preparing the dominant.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: A seventh chord and its four inversions
questions.learningObjective: Compare a seventh chord with a triad in members and positions
questions.stem: The survey writes out a seventh chord in each of its positions. Explain how a seventh chord differs from a triad and how many positions it has.

answer.exemplar: A triad stacks three notes in thirds, so it has a root, a third and a fifth, while a seventh chord adds one more third-built note a seventh above the root. That extra chord member gives it four possible bass notes, so the seventh chord has four inversions: root position, first, second and third inversion.

questions.explanation: Adding a third-built seventh above the root turns a triad into a seventh chord, and the extra chord member creates a fourth possible bass note. Hence four positions rather than the triad's three.
questions.hint: Count the members, then the bass choices.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: A seventh chord and its four inversions
questions.learningObjective: Explain the third inversion of a seventh chord
questions.stem: The survey records a seventh chord whose seventh is the lowest sounding note. Explain how that chord is described and what makes it different from a triad inversion.

answer.exemplar: The chord is in third inversion, because a seventh chord's position is named by which of its four members sits in the bass, and here that member is the seventh. Unlike a triad, which has three members and therefore three positions, a seventh chord adds a fourth member, so a seventh can come to rest in the bass and the chord has a distinct third inversion.

questions.explanation: A seventh chord has four members, so its bass can be the root, third, fifth or seventh, giving four positions. With the seventh in the bass the chord is in third inversion, a position no triad can reach.
questions.hint: The bass member names the position.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Subdominant and dominant function
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish dominant function from subdominant function
questions.stem: The survey annotates phrase endings with functional labels. Explain the difference between dominant and subdominant function.

answer.exemplar: Dominant function carries the drive toward the tonic, so the dominant chord, usually built on the fifth degree, is the one that creates the expectation of a return and resolves back to the tonic. Subdominant function does the opposite work: the subdominant chord, built on the fourth degree, points away from the tonic and prepares the dominant, which is why a phrase moves from tonic to subdominant to dominant and then home.

questions.explanation: The dominant pushes toward the tonic and resolves back to it, while the subdominant prepares the dominant and points away. A phrase usually runs tonic, subdominant, dominant, tonic.
questions.hint: One pulls home, the other prepares.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of the raised seventh in a minor key
questions.stem: The survey transcribes a minor-key phrase whose seventh degree sounds a semitone below the tonic. Explain how that note affects the phrase.

answer.exemplar: In a minor key the seventh degree is normally a whole step below the tonic, so raising it by a semitone creates the leading tone. questions.explanation: Raising the seventh degree by a semitone places it a half step below the tonic, and that narrow gap gives the note its upward pull. It is the source of the tension that makes minor keys sound unsettled.

questions.topic: What a key signature holds
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a key signature carries and how it is applied
questions.stem: The survey needs to explain key signatures to a new field assistant. Explain what information a key signature carries and how it is applied.

answer.exemplar: A key signature is a set of accidentals attached to letter names, and it applies as a standing instruction to every occurrence of those letters wherever they appear in the piece. A sharp on F therefore raises every F unless a written accidental cancels it for that note or measure. The signature also fixes the pool of pitches available, which is what allows the key, its relatives and its scale to be inferred from it.

questions.explanation: A key signature collects accidentals under the staff and applies them to matching letter names throughout the piece. It therefore constrains which pitches are available, though individual notes may override it.
questions.hint: It is a standing instruction, not a list.

answer.exemplar: In a minor key the seventh degree sits a whole step below the tonic, which gives it little pull, so it is raised by a semitone to create the leading tone. questions.explanation: Raising the seventh degree places it a half step below the tonic, and that narrow gap gives the note its upward pull. It is the source of the tension that makes minor keys sound unsettled.
